name: PURE Asian National Title
notes: Attested by the fed's own division rankings (/promotions/pure/archive/columns.html) and by its own news page, which reports a first-round tournament match at Ikusa III (/promotions/pure/archive/news.html). PURE ran a separately-named PURE All-Asia Championship through the first three months of 2003, whose own first holder is billed on his own roster card as "First Ever Pure All Asia Champion"; whether that belt is this one renamed or a second championship is not settled by the record, and the two are held as distinct titles. Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).
epitaph: A belt PURE ran a tournament for and never crowned inside the surviving record. Its own columnist argued the division belonged to Inphino Blitz on three counts and then argued against himself, calling it a bit of an oxymoron to have a gaijin as Asian National Champion; three of the four other men he ranked in it — Shirata Rinjiro, Masanobu Ozaki and Steven Windsor — were released within three weeks. The fed's own pay-per-view announcement of 21 May 2002 promised the first Asian Champion would be named at Future Destinies, alongside the first World Champion. The held record stops before either.

name: PURE Jr. Heavyweight Title
notes: Attested by the fed's own Ikusa IV card, which bills a defence (/promotions/pure/archive/ikusa-4-card.html), and by its own division rankings (/promotions/pure/archive/columns.html). Its whole lineage is the fed's own: a complete Junior Heavyweight Championship history of six numbered reigns, served at /promotions/pure/archive/junior-heavyweight-championship-history.html. Its champions page carries only the holder of the moment — "Champion: El Romantico" in its January 2003 state, "Champion: Radiant" in its last — and Radiant's own roster card carries the only dated list of defences any PURE belt has. The history and the show scripts disagree twice, and both stand each time: the history names Ikusa III for the change of 16 June 2002 that the Ikusa V script carries, and it has Charlie Loc pin The End for the belt on 28 July 2002 where PCW's own Wrestle Vessel script has him pin Alexander Miyagawa for it. Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).
epitaph: The first belt PURE awarded, and the only one it carried through both of its runs. The End won it on 28 April 2002 at Ikusa II in Matsumoto, beating The H.I.T. and Kensuke Suzahara in a three-way the fed billed as the crowning of its first ever champion. He lost it seven weeks later at Ikusa V in the Sapporo Dome, pinned by The H.I.T. in a tag match the fed put his title on, with The H.I.T. announced in the ring as the new champion, and won it back that summer in a fatal four-way over Inphino Blitz that PURE's own title history places on a show called Ikusa 6 and does not date. It left him for good on 28 July 2002, in another federation's ring: Charlie Loc took it in the first fall of a two-fall match at PCW's Wrestle Vessel that carried the PURE Junior Heavyweight and PCW Cruiserweight titles at once, and was billed afterwards as the first man to win a PURE title outside a PURE ring. He lost it on 13 October 2002 to a masked DJ Nygma, unmasked in the ring that night as El Romantico, who was still champion and under contract to another federation when PURE re-opened. PURE decided the belt again by tournament in January 2003, and Radiant won it on the 26th at Hakatanomori Football Stadium, beating Isao Asai in thirty minutes and fifteen seconds. He beat Asai twice more, then wrestled El Mesias to a draw at Budokan Hall on 9 March 2003, and the surviving record carries no later change.

name: PURE Tag Team Titles
notes: Attested by the fed's own division rankings, which name a PURE Tag Team Title Tournament as forthcoming (/promotions/pure/archive/columns.html), and by its own title-history page, rendered from newsdata board 52's neighbour board 78: "#1 - Mang-A-Hero and Inphino Blitz. Defeated the team of Ebola III and Alexander Miyagawa to win the belts at Ikusa V." Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).
epitaph: PURE's original tag team titles, awarded once and never defended. Inphino Blitz and Mang-A-Hero won them on 16 June 2002 at Ikusa V in the Sapporo Dome, beating Ebola III and the fed's own owner Alexander Miyagawa in a match booked on air as the first awarding of the belts. No other team held them: PURE retired them when it re-opened in January 2003 and declared a three-man Trinity Tag Team Championship in their place. Mang-A-Hero, on commentary a year later, called himself and his partner the first and last PURE Tag Team Champions.

events.note: PURE's own title-history page, in its own words: "#2 - Titles retired. Retired belts upon the reopening of PURE." Its own show commentary says the same from the other side — "We were the FIRST AND LAST PURE TAG TEAM CHAMPIONS!" / "That's only because Mina retired that spot for the Trinity!" The Trinity Tag Team Titles declared in their place are their own title row, not a continuation of this lineage.

name: PURE World Heavyweight Championship
notes: Attested by the fed's own title-history page (/promotions/pure/archive/world-heavyweight-championship-history.html) and by its own division rankings (/promotions/pure/archive/columns.html). That page is rendered from newsdata board 78 and was rewritten in place three times: the held copy reads "#1 - To be determined at 'Future Destinies' (8/14/02)"; the deposit's January 2003 layer reads "#1 - To be determined at a later date (???)"; and the deposit's last layer no longer carries this belt at all, having been overwritten with the tag titles' own history. Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).
epitaph: PURE announced a World Heavyweight Championship in 2002 and did not award it. The fed built a championship-history page for the belt and filled it with a single line — a first champion to be determined at a pay-per-view in the Tokyo Dome — and rewrote that line twice without ever naming a holder; the belt was still vacant when PURE re-opened in January 2003. It was decided on 2 March 2003 at Final Destinies, in the Tokyo Dome after all, by a four-man tournament Jesse Ramey won over Eddie Mandrake. Ramey defended it a week later at Budokan Hall against Jason Marah, and the surviving record carries no later change.

name: PURE All-Asia Championship
epitaph: A championship PURE ran through the last three months of its record, and the one belt it moved between its two touring brands. Senji Yulav was its first champion, billed as such from the fed's own January 2003 shows onward. Kohana took it from him at Final Destinies in the Tokyo Dome on 2 March 2003, by submission. A week later at Budokan Hall, Raizo Tenzan beat Kohana for it in ten minutes and thirty-nine seconds, in a match PURE booked to settle which of its two brands the belt would follow; Tenzan took it from the referee's hands rather than be presented with it. The surviving record carries no later change.
notes: Attested by PURE's own show scripts for Final Destinies (2 March 2003) and the Budokan Ikusa (9 March 2003), by its own news rows of 7 and 18 February 2003, and by the roster cards for Senji Yuvlav ("First Ever Pure All Asia Champion") and Raizo Tenzan. Whether this belt is the same championship as the PURE Asian National Title the fed ran a tournament for in May 2002 is not settled by the record: the names differ, the eras do not overlap, and Yuvlav's own card calls him the first ever holder. Filed as a distinct title, and the question is recorded rather than answered.

name: PURE Trinity Tag Team Titles
epitaph: The three-man tag team championship PURE instated when it re-opened in January 2003, in place of the two-man tag titles it retired at the same time. Shaun Styles and the Sushi Crew were its first champions, beating the Black Dragons for the belts. The Suburban Ninja Clan took them at Budokan Hall on 9 March 2003, and eight days later answered with an open challenge to any three-man team in the federations PURE shared a host with, offering to defend the belts on those feds' own shows. The surviving record carries no later change.
notes: Instated on PURE's own studio show Axcess, in the fed's own words: "PURE has now instated the brand new PURE Trinity Tag Team titles. Puro wrestling is quite famous for their 6 man tag team action and it was only a matter of time before we embraced that staple of the culture." Its lineage sits at the tail of the same title-history page that carries the two-man tag titles' (newsdata board 78, the page world.shtml renders): "#3 - Trinity Tag Team Championship declared. Sushi Crew / Shaun Styles become new champions over Black Dragons." Source: Argyle's PURE deposit (collection 0159).
